name: Tootgarook
intro: Tootgarook is a small, mostly residential village squeezed between Rye and Capel Sound, and its real identity lives behind the streets in the Tootgarook Wetland  -  the largest privately-protected freshwater wetland on the Peninsula and a quiet ecological headline most visitors do not know exists. Out front, the village sits across the road from a wide bay beach with shallow water and a long pier; out back, the wetland soaks into the dunes and the migratory bird counts each spring are among the highest on the Peninsula. The village itself has a handful of shops and an unfussy main street and is almost entirely a place locals use. Stay nearby for cheaper Peninsula accommodation than Rye or Sorrento; come to walk the wetland boardwalk and read birds in the reeds.
factualLede: Tootgarook is a small village on the Mornington Peninsula's southern Port Phillip coast between Rye and Capel Sound, 80 km from Melbourne, with a calm bay beach across the highway and the Tootgarook Wetland reserve behind the dunes.

tldr: Tootgarook is a quiet bayside village with the Peninsula's largest freshwater wetland reserve behind the dunes.
Best for: birders; budget weekenders looking for a Rye-adjacent base; families using the bay beach.
Signature experience: a spring morning walking the Tootgarook Wetland boardwalk, then a swim from the bayside pier.
A weekend; pair with Rye, Boneo and the back beaches for a full Peninsula loop.
There is little to eat in the village — walk into Rye for restaurants.
notFor: anyone wanting a dining scene at the doorstep
first-time Peninsula visitors with one day
signature: A modest bayside village hiding the Peninsula's largest freshwater wetland behind its dunes.
skip: Driving past on the highway — pull off, find the wetland boardwalk, and the village becomes interesting fast.
bestDay: Dawn walk on the Tootgarook Wetland boardwalk, late breakfast in Rye, midday swim from the bayside pier, afternoon back-beach detour, dinner in Rye.
insiderNote: Tootgarook Wetland is one of the Peninsula's most important migratory bird sites — bring binoculars in spring and bird lists in summer.
